title: Top 3 Return-to-Office Metrics You Can Track Without Badges or Sensors
summary: Track office-day compliance, desk utilisation, and team coordination without badges or sensors. Learn the formulas, data limits, and practical next steps.
body_markdown:
## What These Return-to-Office Metrics Can and Cannot Tell You


Hybrid policies create two practical needs: apply office-day expectations consistently and plan enough workspace for the people coming in. You can answer many of these operational questions without installing badges, Wi-Fi tracking, or occupancy sensors.


Slack or Microsoft Teams-native desk booking lets employees reserve desks, see who plans to attend, and coordinate office days inside familiar collaboration tools. This approach reduces the need for a separate workplace app and supports everyday planning (learn more about[hybrid work software](https://getofficely.com/solutions/hybrid-work-software) ).


The distinction between each data source matters:


- Bookings show that someone planned to attend and reserve capacity.
- Manual check-ins show reported participation in an office day.
- Badges, Wi-Fi, and sensors provide stronger evidence that someone physically arrived. Depending on the system, they can also measure real-time presence or use.


These signals are related, but they are not interchangeable. Check-in methods can include an app, office Wi-Fi, occupancy sensors, or connected access systems, and the strength of the arrival evidence depends on the method[\[1\]](https://www.inkl.com/news/8-best-desk-booking-software-platforms-in-2026) .


This guide focuses on operational hybrid-policy management, workplace planning, and team coordination. It does not cover legal or regulatory compliance, employee surveillance, productivity scoring, or enterprise facilities management.


The three return-to-office metrics to track are:


- Office-day compliance rate
- Desk and space utilisation
- Team coordination rate


Together, they help you understand whether agreed attendance expectations are being met, whether reserved capacity matches demand, and whether teams are spending planned office days together.


## The Top 3 Return-to-Office Metrics to Track


Use the same definitions across each reporting period. A stable method lets you compare like with like and spot changes that need attention.


Metric Calculation What the data represents Recommended cadence Operational decision supported


Office-Day Compliance Rate Employees meeting the minimum office days ÷ employees covered by the policy × 100 Attendance against an operational hybrid-work policy Each policy reporting period Policy administration and follow-up


Desk and Space Utilisation Booked desk-days ÷ available desk-days × 100; confirmed-use desk-days ÷ available desk-days × 100 where a consistent check-in signal exists Reserved capacity or reported use over time Regular review by reporting period Desk supply and space planning


Team Coordination Rate Planned team office days with required teammates together ÷ planned team office days × 100 Team overlap on intended collaboration days Each team planning period Shared office days and team seating


### Office-Day Compliance Rate


Office-day compliance rate measures the share of covered employees who meet the minimum in-office expectation during a defined reporting period. It is an operational policy-administration measure, not a statement about legal compliance.


Numerator: Employees who meet the minimum number of in-office days during the reporting period.


Denominator: Employees covered by that policy during the same period.


Data source: Desk bookings and Slack or Microsoft Teams check-ins can provide participation records. Approved remote exceptions must be excluded or handled through one documented method. Officely can log attendance, compare it with a hybrid-work policy, and flag gaps for managers (see[the Officely review](https://peoplemanagingpeople.com/tools/officely-review) )[\[2\]](https://peoplemanagingpeople.com/tools/officely-review) .


Cadence: Calculate the rate at the end of each policy reporting period. Use the same period defined in the policy, such as its stated weekly or monthly cycle.


Hypothetical calculation: A policy covers 40 employees after approved exceptions are accounted for. If 34 meet the minimum office-day requirement, the calculation is:


34 ÷ 40 × 100 = 85%


This is an illustrative example, not a benchmark.


Example interpretation: The result shows that 85% of covered employees recorded enough qualifying office days during that period. It does not explain why the remaining employees fell below the requirement.


What to do next: Review exceptions, incomplete records, and unclear expectations before contacting managers or employees. Repeated gaps may indicate that a policy needs clarification or that the chosen office days do not suit the team’s operating needs.


This metric replaces scattered spreadsheet checks with one consistent calculation. It also gives managers a starting point for follow-up without treating every missing booking as deliberate non-participation.


### Desk and Space Utilisation


Desk and space utilisation measures demand for workspace over a chosen period. To interpret it correctly, separate bookings, actual use, and occupancy.


- Desk bookings represent reserved capacity. They show intent and planning demand.
- Actual usage indicates whether a reserved or available desk was used, where a consistent check-in or arrival signal exists.
- Occupancy compares the number of people using a space with its capacity at a particular point in time.


Occupancy is a snapshot. Utilisation measures how much space is used across a longer period, such as the reporting cycle defined by your workplace team (see[the office-utilisation metrics guide](https://getofficely.com/blog/office-utilization-metrics-guide) ).


Numerator: For booked-desk utilisation, use booked desk-days. For actual-use utilisation, use desk-days with a completed check-in or another consistent confirmation of use.


Denominator: Available desk-days during the chosen period.


Data source: Booking records provide intent and planning data. Completed check-ins or consistent arrival signals provide participation or arrival data. A booking alone does not prove that someone used the desk.


Cadence: Review utilisation regularly across comparable periods. Use a cadence that supports desk allocation, capacity planning, and booking-rule decisions.


Hypothetical calculation: An office has 200 available desk-days during a reporting period. Employees reserve 150 desk-days.


150 ÷ 200 × 100 = 75% booked-desk utilisation


If 120 desk-days also have a completed check-in:


120 ÷ 200 × 100 = 60% actual-use utilisation


Both calculations are illustrative. They show different parts of the booking process rather than company benchmarks.


Example interpretation: The difference between the booked and checked-in figures suggests that some reserved capacity did not have confirmed use. It does not prove that every unchecked booking was unused, because employees may forget to check in.


No-shows can create ghost bookings, where a desk remains reserved despite sitting empty. Check-in processes can release unused desks when configured with appropriate release rules (see[the desk-booking software guide](https://getofficely.com/solutions/desk-booking-software) ).


What to do next: Review booking guidance, check-in completion, desk release rules, and demand by office day. A persistent booking-to-use gap may call for clearer cancellation habits or a better release process. Consistently high demand may justify changing desk availability or helping teams spread attendance across suitable days.


Hardware-based systems are useful when you need physical-presence evidence or granular, real-time occupancy data. Sensors can reveal information such as desk popularity and duration of use. Bookings and manual check-ins support a lighter approach when your questions concern planned demand and reported participation.


### Team Coordination Rate


Team coordination rate measures whether the right colleagues plan or report attendance together on designated team office days. It focuses on useful overlap instead of counting individual attendance in isolation.


Before calculating the rate, define required teammates. Depending on the purpose of the office day, this group could be:


- The whole team
- A project pod
- A minimum collaboration group
- Specific roles needed for a planned activity


Apply that definition consistently throughout the reporting period.


Numerator: Planned team office days when the required teammates are booked or checked in together.


Denominator: All planned team office days during the reporting period.


Data source: Team-day schedules, desk bookings, and check-in records from Slack or Microsoft Teams. Team neighbourhood or seating information can show whether colleagues planned to sit near one another.


Cadence: Calculate the rate for each team planning period. Align the review with how often the team agrees or revises its shared office days.


Hypothetical calculation: A project pod has eight planned collaboration days in a reporting period. The required group is booked or checked in together on six days.


6 ÷ 8 × 100 = 75%


This example illustrates the formula and is not a recommended target.


Example interpretation: The required collaboration group overlapped on six of its eight intended office days. The metric shows coordination against the plan. It does not show whether the team was productive or whether each day produced a specific business result.


What to do next: Help the team choose shared days that work for the required group. Where seating affects the purpose of the day, use team neighbourhoods or team-based seating arrangements to help colleagues reserve desks near one another.


A low coordination rate may mean people are attending on different days, even when individual office-day compliance is high. That distinction helps you improve collaboration plans without increasing the attendance requirement.


## How to Collect the Data in Slack or Microsoft Teams


A hardware-free workflow should feel like ordinary office planning. The purpose is to make attendance easier to coordinate, not to catch people out.


Officely operates inside Slack and Microsoft Teams, where employees can book desks, check who is coming in, and coordinate office days without leaving those tools.


1. Publish the policy and planned team days. Explain who the policy covers, the reporting period, the minimum expectation, and how exceptions work.
2. Ask employees to reserve desks. Let employees record their planned attendance through Slack or Microsoft Teams.
3. Collect check-ins where your process uses them. Explain what counts as a completed check-in and how employees should correct a missed record.
4. Calculate the three metrics. Review office-day compliance, desk and space utilisation, and team coordination on a regular cadence.
5. Discuss patterns with the right owner. Share relevant findings with the responsible manager, People team, or workplace owner and agree on an operational action.


Hybrid-work software can also provide analytics on desk reservations, meeting-room bookings, and daily attendance. For these three metrics, keep the analysis focused on desk booking, attendance or check-ins, and team overlap.


Reporting may show patterns by policy group, location, or team when those views are needed for policy administration and space planning. Avoid collecting or dividing data into extra categories without a clear operational reason.


## Use the Metrics Fairly and Consistently


### Create Clear Policy Rules Before Reporting


Fair reporting starts with documented definitions. Write the rules before reviewing individual or team results.


Define:


- Who is covered by the policy
- The minimum in-office expectation
- The start and end of each reporting period
- Which office locations count
- How approved remote exceptions are handled
- What counts as a completed booking
- What counts as a completed check-in
- How cancellations and corrected records affect the calculation


These are operational rules rather than legal advice. Their purpose is to help comparable employee groups receive the same treatment.


Use one calculation method for each comparable group and communicate it before the first review. If different groups have different attendance expectations, calculate their results against the policy that applies to them.


A metric should prompt a conversation and an operational improvement. It should not become a standalone judgment about an employee’s commitment or performance.


### Turn Patterns Into Better Hybrid-Work Decisions


Each metric points to a different type of action:


- Low office-day compliance: Confirm the records, resolve approved exceptions, and clarify the attendance expectation.
- A large booking-to-use gap: Review cancellations, check-in completion, desk release rules, and booking guidance.
- Low team coordination: Help the team agree on shared office days and suitable neighbourhood arrangements.


Look at several reporting periods before making a large space or policy change. A single period may contain holidays, office closures, team events, or temporary project demands.


Attendance also provides only one view of hybrid work. Broader reviews can include employee engagement, satisfaction, and feedback.[How to Schedule Support Teams Returning to Office](https://getofficely.com/blog/encourage-employees-return-office) recommends gathering input through anonymous surveys, informal check-ins, or hybrid-work software data instead of relying only on attendance.


## Data Limitations and Privacy Considerations


Bookings show reservation intent. Manual check-ins show reported participation. Neither provides the same evidence as badge, Wi-Fi, or sensor-based physical-presence data.


Use this checklist before publishing or acting on a report:


- Check cancellations and no-shows. A reserved desk may remain unused.
- Account for shared desks. Confirm how multiple bookings or shifts affect available desk-days.
- Review late arrivals and incomplete check-ins. The employee may attend without creating a complete record.
- Find unbooked attendance. Some employees may use the office without reserving a desk.
- Handle office moves consistently. Decide how attendance across multiple eligible locations counts.
- Apply approved remote exceptions. Exclude or account for them through the documented policy method.
- Mark policy changes. A change in required days can make results from different periods hard to compare.
- Record metric definitions. Keep a clear description of each numerator, denominator, data source, and reporting period.
- Collect only necessary data. Retain what you need for hybrid-policy administration and office planning.
- Limit access. Give relevant People, Workplace, and Operations stakeholders access based on their responsibilities.
- Explain the purpose. Tell employees what you collect, how you calculate the metrics, and why you use the results.


Check-ins can use an app, Wi-Fi, occupancy sensors, or connected access systems. Each method provides a different strength of arrival evidence. Document the method instead of labelling every check-in as confirmed physical presence.


Recalculate historical trends carefully when policy eligibility, required days, office capacity, team structures, or check-in processes change. Where a fair recalculation is not possible, mark the change and compare only periods that use compatible definitions.


## Make Return-to-Office Reporting Easier to Act On


The three metrics support three distinct decisions:


- Office-day compliance rate supports consistent hybrid-policy administration.
- Desk and space utilisation supports desk capacity and workplace planning.
- Team coordination rate supports shared office days and coordinated collaboration.


Use hardware-derived data when your operational question requires physical-presence evidence or highly granular, real-time occupancy information. Use Slack or Microsoft Teams bookings and check-ins when you need to understand whether employees planned, reported, and coordinated office attendance.
